reason: 'The same technology shows up as a control on one side and a weapon on the other' only fits one item: encryption (a confidentiality control) used by ransomware. It marks the ransomware item as the trap and rules out Confidentiality for it, so a learner who doesn't get the concept is left with a 50/50 between Integrity and Availability. The first sentence is a sound method; the second points straight at one item.

factual_problem: The hint asks two opposite questions ('noticed first' and 'suffering without knowing') and never says which one decides the bucket. The prompt's test is which property is 'primarily attacked', and when the victim notices is not that test. Read the second way, it can push ransomware toward Confidentiality (silent double-extortion exfiltration).
reason: Keyword shortcut: 'without knowing' matches 'silently altered' word for word, so the payroll item goes to Integrity without understanding. 'Noticed first' points loud events (flood, ransomware) to Availability. Because the decision rule is ambiguous, the hint misleads as much as it leaks.

factual_problem: It narrows Privacy to 'holding less data in the first place', which is data minimisation only. Privacy also covers individuals' rights and control over their data: consent, erasure, purpose and use limitation.
reason: The three glosses paraphrase the items. 'Holding less data' points at 'Collecting only the data fields the service actually needs' and at 'erase what you hold', so both go to Privacy by word match. 'Making an action undeniable afterwards' points at the signed payment and the after-the-fact audit log. 'Establishing who someone is' takes the rest. All six can be placed by keyword matching.
It warns that side effects exist (signing also authenticates; audit logs depend on authentication) but doesn't name which items or which bucket wins. You still need to know what each measure is for.

factual_problem: 'A rule that people follow' is narrower than administrative controls, which also include processes run by people (background checks, training, separation of duties). Background checks fit this gloss only loosely and could look like 'no bucket fits'.
reason: It restates the three type definitions. 'Barrier in the physical world' pins the fence and door, but those are trivial from the bucket name anyway. The firewall's 'by rule' wording is a possible false match to 'rule', but 'people follow' rules that out. Close to a pure method; adds little beyond the definitions.
Repeats the prompt's type-vs-function warning and points to no item. Redundant with the prompt; it costs quality for almost no new information.

factual_problem: 'Who is primarily being protected' misroutes Canon II items. Refusing an unauthorised scan protects the network owner (looks like I or III), and refusing to exaggerate protects the prospect (looks like III). Canon II is about your own conduct (honesty, legality), not about protecting a party. The criterion also clashes with the prompt's 'subject matter' framing.
reason: It is a keyword funnel. 'The public' points at patients and the city dispatch system (I); 'the client who hired you' points at the two items that contain the word 'client' (III); 'the profession' points at ISC2 exam questions and mentoring (IV). Most of this leak is already in the prompt's glosses, so the hint adds little except a misleading criterion for Canon II.
A generic 'fundamentally about' method that names no item or canon. Mostly repeats the prompt's note.

The hint does nothing. 'Assess likelihood x impact' and 'rank' are in the SAME item, so 'can't rank before judging likelihood/cost' says nothing about the order of the five steps. No leak, but it breaks the standing rule against a hint that changes nothing about the learner's approach while still costing quality. Retarget it, e.g. at why identification must come before assessment.

factual_problem: 'Something always remains' is the standard teaching, but avoidance can bring a specific risk's residual close to zero. Minor.
reason: It pins the last position: 'remains afterwards' plus 'named owner' paraphrases 'Document the residual risk and have it formally accepted', so that item goes 5th by word match. It also says outright that Choose is not last. Once the 5th slot is pinned, the rest is easy (Identify -> Assess -> Choose -> Apply is the obvious reading order of the verbs).

factual_problem: 'Policy states an intention' undersells it: policies are mandatory management directives. This framing pushes the mandatory but non-specific 'Every system must have a named owner' toward Standard.
reason: It is a full decision tree that maps one cue to each layer: 'from outside' -> HIPAA; 'optional' -> 'Where practical, prefer'; 'sequence of actions' -> the 'Step 1/2/3' item and the 'click Report, then forward' item. Four of eight items can be placed by surface cue. Still needed: Policy vs Standard on the 'must' items.

factual_problem: 'Detailed and optional' is not a reliable description of a guideline. Guidelines are usually general recommendations, and procedures are detailed but mandatory, so the axis pair blurs the line between guideline and procedure.
reason: 'Mandatory and vague' gives a direct rule for the hardest split. It sends 'must have a named owner' and 'will protect confidentiality' to Policy, and the specific 'must' items (AES-256, hardened OS image) to Standard. Combined with hint 0, the force-by-specificity grid places every item by wording cues (must/will/prefer/step) without understanding the purpose of each layer.
